notes.meaning: Paul tells every believer to submit to the civil government because God is the one who sets up human authorities. God created civil rule to prevent chaos and keep order in society. When Christians respect lawful rulers, they are honoring God's own plan for the world.

differ.view: God governs the world through two distinct kingdoms, using civil rulers and laws to keep outward peace rather than to make people righteous inside.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: John Chrysostom taught that God established the office of governing itself to preserve order, and even church leaders must submit to civil authority.

notes.meaning: Anyone who opposes the rightful authority of the government is rebelling against what God has established. People who choose that path bring punishment on themselves from both the civil courts and God. Believers should avoid stirring up needless rebellion and seek to live in peace.

differ.view: Believers must obey civil magistrates as ministers of God, disobeying only when a ruler commands something that directly breaks God's law.
Christians must not resist government authority unless they are using lawful means provided by the legal system of the community.

notes.meaning: Paul explains that rulers are generally meant to punish evil deeds rather than good ones. People who obey the law have no reason to be terrified of those in power. By doing what is right, citizens can expect protection and approval from their leaders.

The civil ruler acts as a servant of God to protect people and encourage good behavior. The sword represents the government's power to punish criminals and enforce justice. When rulers carry out just penalties against wrongdoers, they are serving God's purpose to defend innocent people.

Christians must obey the authorities for two important reasons. They obey not only to escape legal punishment, but also to keep a clear conscience before God. Doing what is right should come from a willing heart of obedience to God, not just from the fear of getting caught.

Paying taxes is a duty because government workers spend their time and energy maintaining public order. Their work requires real expense to guard the community and keep peace. Christians support this work fairly by paying the taxes required of them.

Paul tells believers to give every official exactly what is owed to them. This includes property taxes, customs on trade, obedience to lawful authority, and genuine respect for each office. Paying our dues honestly is one clear way to show Christian character in daily life.

Believers should pay off all financial debts so they do not remain indebted to anyone. The only debt a Christian can never completely finish paying is the ongoing debt to love other people. Loving your neighbor fulfills the heart of what God's commandments require.

Paul lists several commandments from the law, including those against adultery, murder, stealing, and coveting. All of these rules about how to treat others are gathered into one simple command: love your neighbor as yourself. A heart full of love will naturally protect others rather than harm them.

True love never seeks to injure or cheat another person. Because love always works for the neighbor's good, it fulfills the entire purpose of God's moral law toward others. Showing genuine love is the greatest way to keep God's commands.

differ.view: Believers strive to love others, but only Christ kept the law completely, so believers rest in Christ's perfection rather than their own performance.
A heart filled with God's love is naturally restrained from doing any evil and moved to do every kind of good toward neighbors.

notes.meaning: Paul urges Christians to wake up from spiritual laziness because time is slipping away. The final day when Christ returns to complete our salvation is closer now than when we first trusted him. Remembering the brevity of life helps us stay alert and active for God.

The dark night of this present evil world is nearly finished, and the bright day of Christ's return is close at hand. Christians should throw off sinful practices just like taking off dirty nightclothes. Instead, they must put on the bright armor of a holy life to stand firm against temptation.

Believers are called to live decently and openly, as people do in the full light of day. Paul warns against wild parties, drunkenness, sexual impurity, and bitter arguments or envy. Our public and private actions should be things we are never ashamed to bring into the light.

Instead of planning ways to satisfy sinful cravings, believers are commanded to clothe themselves with the Lord Jesus Christ. This means relying on him and letting his character shape how we live each day. Walking closely with Jesus guards our minds against feeding sinful desires.

differ.view: Putting on Christ describes the believer's intimate union with Jesus, being clothed with all the holy graces and virtues seen in him.
Putting on Christ includes both receiving his imputed righteousness as a covering before God and putting on holy conduct for daily life.
